newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Peronist senator whips up new "Menem '99" storm.
newsitem.headline: Peronist senator whips up new "Menem '99" storm.

text.p: Argentina's Peronist government tried on Saturday to play down speculation of a third consecutive election bid for President Carlos Menem in 1999, after Senator Jorge Yoma proposed legalising plebiscites to allow the constitution to the changed.

Yoma scared the opposition by announcing he would launch a bill when Congress resumes in February to give legal status to plebiscites, which are allowed under the constitution but have never been passed into law.

Such a referendum would "exclude no issues, not even reforming the constitution," Peronist Sen. Yoma said. This was interpreted as a sign he wants to change statutes that currently block Menem from running for a third consecutive term. Menem got the constitution changed in 1994 to let him seek a second term -- which he won hands-down in 1995.

But the Peronist whip in the lower house of Congress, Jorge Matzkin, told reporters: "I don't know exactly what Jorge Yoma is up to, but I would say it is not an issue we are analysing at this moment."
Menem has said repeatedly he will leave office in 1999 and wait until 2004 to try again for the presidency. Yoma acknowledged that Menem "has no political desire" to seek another term.
But that did not reassure the opposition, which believes Menem is keeping his options open.

CGT labour federation boss Rodolfo Daer said such a bid by Menem loyalists was just an attempt to "distract us from the real problem" and added that he believes Menem will retire to his native La Rioja in 1999. But he did appear to leave open the possibility of a third Menem bid if this October's mid-term Congressional elections are favourable for the Peronist president.
"If these things gel or not will be expressed through elections and the main barometer will be in October," said Daer.
From the business sector there was open encouragement for the Peronist president, who has brought free-market reforms and unaccustomed stability since he was first elected in 1989.

"If popular demand is imposed via a plebiscite, because there is no one who has his capacity to keep running the country, with the unequivocal wishes of the Congress, then I don't think it would be a bad thing," said Jorge Blanco Villegas of the Argentine Industrial Union business lobby.
